title: Maurice Wilkes and the First Cache Memory Paper (1965)
explainer: In April 1965, Maurice Wilkes - who had earlier helped build EDSAC, one of the first stored-program computers - published "Slave Memories and Dynamic Storage Allocation," the first paper describing what we now call a cache: a small, fast memory that transparently holds copies of recently used data from a larger, slower main memory. Wilkes called it a "slave memory"; the name we use now, cache, comes from the French word for "to hide," describing a hidden layer that makes slow memory look fast. It is the direct ancestor of the L1/L2/L3 hierarchy you are measuring empirically in this lesson.

resources.title: Maurice Wilkes Introduces Memory Caching, Giving it a Name No Longer Politically Correct

title: Denning's Working Set Model and the Principle of Locality
explainer: While studying thrashing in MIT's Multics time-sharing system in the 1960s, Peter Denning formalized "locality of reference" - the empirical observation that a running program tends to repeatedly touch a small, slowly-shifting subset of its memory rather than accessing it uniformly - into the working set model, described in his 1967 paper and 1968 thesis. That principle is the entire reason a small, fast cache can speed up access to a much larger memory at all: if real programs touched memory uniformly at random, no cache hierarchy would help. When you empirically measure cache hit rates in this lesson, you are directly measuring how strongly a program's real access pattern exhibits the locality Denning described.
